ratings.reviewer_notes: Direct review of HBV-associated hepatocarcinogenesis covering chronic inflammation, fibrosis/cirrhosis, accelerated hepatocyte turnover, HBV integration, viral mutants, replication, and HBx/preS2 oncoproteins.

Characterizes the immunosuppressive, exhausted immune microenvironment of established HBV-related HCC, including PD-1-positive TREG and resident-memory CD8 T cells; informative for immune mechanisms but not tumor initiation.
Mechanism-focused review addressing chronic inflammation/cirrhosis, viral load, HBV mutation and integration, host factors, and HBx-mediated disruption of proliferation and apoptosis pathways.

Maps HBV- and HBx-responsive microRNAs and their regulatory targets across infection, inflammation, fibrosis, cirrhosis, and HCC, providing a specific epigenetic/transcriptional mechanism for progression.

Explains viral-hepatitis-driven inflammation and fibrogenesis through stellate cells, cytokines, immune cells, microRNAs, and epigenetic regulation; fibrosis is an intermediate mechanism, but HCC development is not the main focus.

Direct tumor study showing preferential HBV integration, recurrent TERT-promoter integration associated with increased TERT expression, HBx structural alterations, and expression of HBx-human chimeric products.

Directly reviews the multistep link from HBV to HCC through chronic inflammation/regeneration, viral integration, and transforming activities of HBx and truncated preS2/S proteins, including occult infection.
Comprehensive mechanism review focused on how HBx perturbs cellular signaling and modulates HCC initiation, progression, invasion, and metastasis.

Tests a proposed HBV/HBx-to-HIF mechanism. Hypoxia-responsive genes were induced in chronic HBV patients but not directly by HBV or HBx in infection models, implicating inflammatory mediators instead.
Review specifically describes how ncRNAs mediate HBV/cccDNA effects in HCC through transcriptional regulation, miRNA-sponging, signaling pathways, and RNA/G-quadruplex structures.

Direct review of HBV-associated HCC pathogenesis, including inflammation and cytokine-driven fibrosis/proliferation, insertional effects of integrated HBV DNA, and HBx promotion of cell growth and survival.

Direct functional study identifies a precise integration mechanism: HBV enhancer I inserted at the TERT promoter recruits host ELF4, activates TERT transcription and telomerase, and promotes sphere formation.

Direct mouse and cell-line evidence that HBV protein expression can cause HCC without inflammation or fibrosis; reduced tumor incidence with defective HBx and abrogation by hepatocyte STAT3 knockout support an HBx-STAT3 mechanism.

Directly reviews indirect immune-mediated inflammation/regeneration and direct insertional mutagenesis, HBx/LHBs activity, genomic instability, and characteristic genetic alterations in HBV-related HCC.

Mechanism-focused review covering repeated inflammation, fibrosis and immune dysfunction, HBV DNA integration and genomic instability, fusion proteins, and HBx/HBs effects on apoptosis, signaling, and epigenetics.
Direct genomic study demonstrates oncogenic consequences of HBV integration, including enhancer-driven oncogene overexpression and integration-associated rearrangements affecting TERT, TP53, and MYC.

Direct comparative study evaluates integration as a causal mechanism. Similar integration patterns in tumor and non-tumor tissue argue that most integrations are not associated with carcinogenesis, while documenting rare cancer-gene insertions and truncated HBx.

In established non-cirrhotic HBV-associated HCC, links inflammation and fibrosis to proliferative signaling, Th17 enrichment, PD-L1 expression, reduced tumor-killing immunity, aggressive behavior, and poor prognosis; primarily addresses progression after HCC.

Directly summarizes indirect inflammation-damage-regeneration mechanisms and direct viral mechanisms involving HBV integration, chromosomal alteration, insertional mutagenesis, genomic instability, and HBx-mediated deregulation.
Reviews how HBx establishes and interacts with a chronic inflammatory tumor microenvironment to regulate HCC initiation, growth, invasion, metastasis, and angiogenesis.
